Based on the healthcare Q&A matches, it appears that active screening in coeliac disease risk groups is considered reasonable rather than harmful. Long-term dietary compliance in screen-detected patients was good, and quality of life and bone mineral density were comparable with those in non-coeliac subjects and the general population.

In fact, a study by the International Association of Diabetes and Pregnancy Study Groups (IADPSG) found that active screening in coeliac disease risk groups is cost-effective. The model takes into account postdelivery counseling and intervention to prevent future diabetes in patients identified with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). This suggests that the benefits of early diagnosis and treatment outweigh the costs.

Additionally, research on gluten tolerance in adult patients with celiac disease has shown that some individuals may develop tolerance to gluten over time. However, further follow-up is needed to determine whether this tolerance is permanent or only a long-term return to latency.

It's also worth noting that studies have found no difference in 25(OH)D levels between normal children and those with coeliac disease when adjusted for body mass index. This suggests that vitamin D deficiency is not a feature of pediatric coeliac disease.

In conclusion, the current evidence suggests that active screening in coeliac disease risk groups is justified and may be cost-effective. Further research is needed to fully understand the mechanisms behind gluten tolerance development and the long-term consequences of early diagnosis and treatment.
